body.text: For Canadian businesses asking about a super allowance benefit amount, this page explains that federal SR&ED relief does not apply a notional income super-deduction multiplier. Instead, the Income Tax Act pools deductible expenditures under section 37 and grants 15% or 35% investment tax credits under section 127, with Bill C-15 doubling the enhanced expenditure limit to $6,000,000.

Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program underwent its most substantial statutory and administrative modernization in more than a decade across 2025 and 2026. Enacted through Bill C-15, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, four foundational legislative amendments now govern taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024): first, the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, raising maximum annual federal cash-refundable credits on current expenditures to $2,100,000; second, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor widened from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, paired with an alternative three-year average annual gross revenue phase-out corridor over the same $15,000,000–$75,000,000 range; third, eligibility for the 35% enhanced refundable ITC expanded beyond Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) to include Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs); and fourth, capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024—together with eligible equipment lease outlays incurred after that date—were restored to both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 ITC base (with unclaimed enhanced capital ITCs refunded in cash at a 40% refundability rate for CCPCs).

Three concurrent federal and provincial developments reshape R&D tax compliance across Canada as of November 2026. Administratively, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional pre-claim approval process through My Business Account—issuing upfront technical eligibility determinations within 8 weeks before project work begins and, according to Budget 2025 implementation briefings, cutting post-filing expenditure review targets from 180 days to 90 days—alongside revised May 2026 editions of Form T661, T2 Schedule 31, and T2 Schedule 49. Legislatively, Federal Budget 2026 (updated November 5, 2026) did not enact a standalone federal patent box regime following 2024 consultations, proposing instead a $930 million five-year SR&ED commercialization expansion (for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day) covering initial regulatory certification studies as well as intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs for patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software. Sub-nationally, provincial alignment has diverged markedly: British Columbia expressly adopted the principal federal Bill C-15 expansions and made its 10% credit permanent, Québec replaced legacy R&D credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 with the consolidated 30% / 20% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), and Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, the Atlantic provinces, and Yukon retain independent caps, bases, and refundability rules.
1. Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution (2024–2026)
1.1 Core Provisions of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

Canada's federal R&D tax incentive system operates through a two-pillar statutory design codified in the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), hereinafter the "ITA") and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, hereinafter the "ITR"). Rather than applying a notional income super-deduction multiplier, federal law separates tax relief into two distinct mechanisms: first, the pooling and deduction of allowable SR&ED expenditures in computing business income under Section 37 of the ITA; and second, the earning of non-refundable or cash-refundable Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) on a taxpayer's "qualified expenditure" pool under Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA.

Under Subsection 37(1) of the ITA—including Paragraph 37(1)(a) (and subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) and (i.1)) for current expenditures alongside restored capital expenditure provisions for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024—a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada accumulates allowable SR&ED outlays in a cumulative expenditure pool. The taxpayer may deduct all or any portion of that pool in computing net income for the current taxation year or carry undeducted pool balances forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years. Subsection 37(8) governs the interpretation of SR&ED expenditures in Canada, establishing the statutory election between the traditional overhead method under Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) (including subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II)) and the proxy overhead method under Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) (subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) through (VI), with subclause (V) governing materials consumed or transformed). Subsections 37(10) through 37(12) establish the timing and irrevocability of the overhead election as well as mandatory prescribed-form filing rules. Remuneration paid to non-arm's-length insiders ("specified employees") is strictly regulated under Subsection 37(9) (which bars bonuses and remuneration based on profits for specified employees) and Subsections 37(9.1) through 37(9.5) (which cap allowable specified-employee SR&ED salaries at five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings [YMPE] and require allocation across associated corporations). In parallel, Subsection 78(4) of the ITA excludes accrued remuneration that remains unpaid more than 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which it was incurred, deeming late-paid wages to be incurred in the subsequent year when paid.

The second statutory pillar, governed by Section 127 and Section 127.1 of the ITA, generates dollar-for-dollar Part I federal tax offsets and cash refunds. Subparagraph 127(5)(a)(i) authorizes a taxpayer to deduct from Part I tax otherwise payable an amount up to their investment tax credit at year-end, encompassing amounts earned on the taxpayer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool for the current year or carried over from preceding taxation years. Subsection 127(9) defines "qualified expenditure," notably bringing the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) elected under Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) into the ITC calculation base even though the PPA never enters the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool. Subsection 248(1) of the ITA sets out the general statutory SR&ED definition, and primary CRA policy (SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, updated October 7, 2026), harmonized Gouvernement du Québec statutory guidance, and Department of Finance Budget 2026 Ways and Means documentation explicitly confirm the three eligible branches of R&D (basic research, applied research, and experimental development) and the two-tier ITC rate structure (15% basic rate plus a 20% enhancement producing a 35% rate for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs).

Related-party contracting and anti-double-counting ("grinding") provisions are enforced through Subsections 127(11) through 127(20) of the ITA. Under Subsections 127(13) through 127(15), a non-arm's-length SR&ED performer (transferor) and payer (transferee) may file a joint agreement in prescribed form (Form T1146) to transfer qualified expenditures from the transferor's pool to the transferee's pool—retaining their underlying current or capital nature under Subsection 127(14)—provided the underlying expenditure was paid by the transferor within 180 days of its taxation year-end and the agreement is filed by the transferor's filing-due date (or within the period permitted for serving a Notice of Objection) under Subsection 127(15). Subsections 127(18) and 127(19) require that any government assistance, non-government assistance, or SR&ED contract payment that a taxpayer (or non-arm's-length party) has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive be deducted from qualified SR&ED expenditures otherwise incurred in the year. Subsection 127(20) allows non-arm's-length parties to allocate assistance reductions via Form T1145, whereas Subsection 127(11) deems expected assistance that goes unreceived and ceases in a later year to be reasonably expected to be a repayment of assistance in that year. Cash refundability of unused current-year ITCs operates through Section 127.1, while Subsections 162(5.1) and 162(5.2) establish statutory penalties for non-compliant claim preparer disclosures in Part 9 of Form T661.

At the regulatory tier, Part XXIX of the ITR (Sections 2900 to 2903) governs overhead attribution, proxy calculations, excluded outlays, and special-purpose buildings. Following the repeal of Subsection 2900(1) (SOR/2000-296, s. 1), Subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) define outlays "directly attributable" to the prosecution of SR&ED and to the upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment under the traditional method, requiring such overhead costs to be both directly related and strictly incremental. Subsection 2900(4) sets the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) at 55% of the directly engaged salary base (in force since 2014, down from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013). Subsection 2900(5) establishes the "all or substantially all" (ASA, 90% or more) inclusion rule for directly engaged salaries under the proxy method; Subsection 2900(6) caps the PPA by reference to overall business deductions; Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) restrict specified-employee inclusions in the PPA salary base across single and associated corporations; and Subsection 2900(9) excludes taxable benefits (ITA ss. 6, 7), late-paid wages (ITA s. 78(4)), bonuses, and profit-based remuneration from the PPA salary base for all employees. Section 2901 addresses prescribed included expenditures, Section 2902 specifies prescribed excluded expenditures, and Section 2903 defines special-purpose buildings.

body.text: 1.2 Enacted Reforms Under the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (Bill C-15)

Accurate verification of Canadian R&D tax law in late 2026 requires tracing the progression from Department of Finance public consultations in 2024 and the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) to the finalized statutory package tabled in Federal Budget 2025 on November 4, 2025 by the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. To legislate those Budget 2025 and 2024 FES tax measures, the federal government introduced Bill C-15 (An Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025; official short title: Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) in the 45th Parliament, 1st Session. Bill C-15 passed First Reading in the House of Commons on November 18, 2025, underwent Standing Committee on Finance review (including ministerial appearances on February 5, 2026), was reported by EY Tax News as substantively enacted for Canadian financial accounting purposes on February 26, 2026, and received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 as Chapter 3 of the Statutes of Canada, 2026.

Although Bill C-15 received Royal Assent in March 2026, its core SR&ED expansions take effect retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, commencing on or after December 16, 2024), while its capital expenditure reinstatement applies to depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 and eligible equipment lease costs first payable or incurred after December 15, 2024. Part 1 of Bill C-15 enacted four structural expansions to the SR&ED regime: doubling the enhanced 35% ITC annual expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000; raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000 while introducing an alternative three-year average gross revenue phase-out corridor over the same $15,000,000–$75,000,000 range; extending the 35% refundable SR&ED ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit; and restoring pre-2014 eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures and equipment lease outlays (reversing the 2012 budget repeal) for both the Section 37 income deduction and the 15% / 35% ITCs.

Because capital property claimed under SR&ED cannot simultaneously be claimed for Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) on Schedule 8, corporate tax planners must weigh restored SR&ED capital treatment against the parallel accelerated CCA and clean-economy tax incentives enacted in Bill C-15. As detailed in EY's legislative summary of Bill C-15, Parliament enacted 100% immediate expensing (100% first-year CCA) for productivity-enhancing assets acquired after April 15, 2024 that become available for use before 2027 across Class 44 (patents or rights to use patented information for a limited or unlimited period), Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment and related systems software), and Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and systems software). Furthermore, for qualifying property acquired on or after January 1, 2025 and available for use before 2034, Bill C-15 reinstated the Reaccelerated Investment Incentive—providing three times the normal first-year CCA deduction where the half-year rule applies (or 1.5 times otherwise) before 2030, phasing out between 2030 and 2033—alongside 100% immediate expensing before 2030 (phased out 2030–2033) for manufacturing or processing machinery and equipment (Class 53), clean energy generation and conservation equipment (Class 43.1), and zero-emission vehicles (Classes 54, 55, and 56), complemented by Budget 2025 immediate expensing proposals for manufacturing and processing buildings and a federal Productivity Mega Deduction highlighted in September 2026. In parallel, Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 broadened the Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC to cover antimony, indium, gallium, germanium, and scandium; extended full Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) ITC rates by five years (pushing lower phase-out rates to 2036–2040); expanded Clean Hydrogen ITC eligibility to methane pyrolysis; modified small nuclear eligibility under the Clean Technology ITC; expanded the Critical Mineral Exploration Tax Credit (adding a 2025–2030 top-up) and extended the Mineral Exploration Tax Credit to March 31, 2027; and amended Income Tax Regulations 3100(1)(b) and 3100(3) (retroactive to January 1, 2022) regarding prescribed tax-shelter benefits.
1.3 Proposed Federal Budget 2026 Commercialization Expansion and Patent Box Status

Whereas Bill C-15 is enacted law in force as of March 26, 2026, Federal Budget 2026 (published with a Notice of Ways and Means Motion and updated through November 5, 2026) proposes a major second phase of SR&ED reform targeting post-R&D commercialization and domestic intellectual property protection. According to Table 1 of the Budget 2026 Tax Measures supplementary report, this commercialization expansion carries a projected five-year federal fiscal cost of $930 million: $25 million in 2026–2027, $200 million in 2027–2028, $245 million in 2028–2029, $225 million in 2029–2030, and $235 million in 2030–2031.

Under existing federal rules, SR&ED eligibility ceases once experimental development concludes, excluding downstream regulatory certification testing and intellectual property filing fees. Effective for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day (2026), Budget 2026 proposes to bring two new commercialization pillars into the SR&ED base. First, under the regulatory and certification requirements expansion, eligible SR&ED activities will broaden to encompass tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to satisfy regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a product or process. To qualify, such validation activities must directly relate to an underlying project that is eligible under existing SR&ED rules, and eligible outlays will span the standard SR&ED expenditure categories—salaries and wages, materials, contracting outlays, overhead, and machinery and equipment. Second, under the intellectual property (IP) protection expansion, eligible SR&ED expenditures will expand to cover costs reasonably incurred to prepare, file, obtain, and periodically maintain legal protection for IP developed during an SR&ED-eligible project across four protected categories (under Canadian legislation or equivalent foreign legislation): patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software. IP enforcement outlays (such as infringement litigation costs) and unrelated legal expenses are strictly excluded. Official administrative fees paid to foreign IP offices qualify, whereas supporting professional services (such as preparing a patent application) qualify only if conducted in Canada. Furthermore, if a taxpayer later disposes of IP for which SR&ED IP-protection support was claimed, statutory recapture rules will apply to claw back the associated SR&ED deduction and ITC amounts.

Tax auditors and corporate counsel should also verify the status of Canada's federal patent box consultation. Although the Department of Finance held formal consultations from January 31, 2024 to April 15, 2024 on establishing a federal patent box regime and indicated in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement that design details would follow, neither Bill C-15 nor Federal Budget 2026 enacted a federal patent box regime. Instead, federal policy as of November 2026 addresses domestic IP commercialization through 100% immediate expensing on Class 44 patent acquisitions, the proposed Budget 2026 SR&ED expansion for regulatory certification and IP registration/maintenance outlays, and a broader federal review of intellectual property frameworks announced in Budget 2026.
2. Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Pool Mechanics
2.1 Basic (15%) and Enhanced (35%) Investment Tax Credit Tiers

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (published October 7, 2026), federal SR&ED ITCs are earned at two statutory rates applied to a claimant's year-end qualified SR&ED expenditure pool after deducting government assistance, non-government assistance, and SR&ED contract receipts. The basic ITC rate of 15% applies generally to corporations (including foreign-controlled subsidiaries, large public corporations, and CCPCs or ECPCs on qualified expenditures exceeding their annual expenditure limit), individuals (sole proprietors), partners in a partnership, and beneficiaries of a trust. The enhanced ITC rate of 35%—comprising the 15% basic rate plus a 20% statutory enhancement—applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures up to a qualifying corporation's annual expenditure limit. Whereas pre-2025 law restricted the 35% enhanced rate exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), Bill C-15 extended the 35% enhanced rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.
2.2 The $6 Million Expenditure Limit and Dual Phase-Out Regimes

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit eligible for the 35% enhanced ITC doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, allowing a qualifying CCPC or ECPC to earn up to $2,100,000 annually in enhanced federal ITCs ($6,000,000 × 35%). Associated CCPCs must share and allocate a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit across all CCPCs in the associated corporate group via T2 Schedule 49, while ECPCs that belong to a consolidated corporate group must similarly allocate a single $6,000,000 limit across the consolidated group.

To prevent high-growth innovators in life sciences, clean technology, advanced manufacturing, and artificial intelligence from losing enhanced-rate access prematurely upon raising institutional capital, Bill C-15 enacted two parallel phase-out methodologies over an expanded $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 corridor for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Under the default Taxable Capital Method available to CCPCs, gradual reduction of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins only when the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs for the previous taxation year reaches $15,000,000, and the expenditure limit becomes nil when prior-year combined taxable capital reaches or exceeds $75,000,000 (replacing the pre–December 16, 2024 corridor of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000). Applying linear reduction across this $60,000,000 statutory phase-out span ($75,000,000 − $15,000,000), every $10 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 limit by $1 (Annual Limit = $6,000,000 × [($75,000,000 − Prior-Year Taxable Capital) ÷ $60,000,000]). Illustratively, a scaling CCPC with $45,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital—whose enhanced limit under the pre-reform $3,000,000 / $10M–$50M corridor shrank to $375,000 ($131,250 at 35%)—retains a $3,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit under the post–December 15, 2024 rules, generating $1,050,000 in 35% ITCs (an eightfold increase).

Alternatively, under the Average Annual Revenue Method, ECPCs are required to use—and CCPCs may elect to use—their average annual gross revenue over the preceding three fiscal years in place of taxable capital. Under this revenue test, gradual reduction of the $6,000,000 limit begins at $15,000,000 of three-year average annual revenue and reaches nil at $75,000,000 or more. Consequently, an equity-financed clinical biotechnology or hardware CCPC carrying more than $75,000,000 in balance-sheet taxable capital (which would reduce its limit to zero under the taxable capital test) that averages under $15,000,000 in gross revenue over its last three fiscal years can elect the revenue-averaging method and preserve its full $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit.
2.3 Refundability Rules Across Entity and Expenditure Classifications

When a claimant has no Part I federal tax otherwise payable (or holds an unclaimed current-year SR&ED ITC balance after offsetting Part I tax), cash refundability under Section 127.1 varies sharply between current-nature expenditures (including the PPA) and capital-nature expenditures, as well as between "Qualifying Corporation" CCPCs, non-qualifying CCPCs, ECPCs, and other claimants. Specifically, CRA's October 7, 2026 SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy confirms that for CCPCs that are Qualifying Corporations (and not Excluded Corporations), unclaimed current-year ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate are 100% refundable on current-nature expenditures and the PPA (producing a 35.0% immediate cash return), but 40% refundable on capital-nature expenditures (producing a 14.0% immediate cash refund [35% × 40%] while leaving 21.0% [35% × 60%] in the non-refundable ITC carryover pool), and 40% refundable on ITCs earned at the 15% basic rate above the expenditure limit (yielding a 6.0% immediate cash refund [15% × 40%] plus 9.0% carryover).

For CCPCs that are NOT Qualifying Corporations (and not Excluded Corporations), unclaimed current-year ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate remain 100% refundable on current-nature expenditures and the PPA and 40% refundable on qualified capital expenditures, whereas ITCs earned at the 15% basic rate are strictly non-refundable (0% cash refund). Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) likewise gain access under Bill C-15 to the 35% refundable SR&ED ITC up to their allocated $6,000,000 expenditure limit for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (100% refundable on current expenditures and the PPA and 40% refundable on capital expenditures), while earning the non-refundable 15% basic rate on excess expenditures. Foreign-controlled subsidiaries, non-eligible public corporations, and corporate partners outside the enhanced regime earn the 15% non-refundable basic ITC, while unincorporated individuals and trusts (where each beneficiary is a qualifying corporation or an individual) earn the 15% basic ITC reported on Form T2038(IND), of which 40% of the unused current-year amount is refundable.

body.text: 2.4 Deductible Expenditure Pool, Carryforwards, Carrybacks, and Acquisition of Control

Multi-year pool management under Sections 37, 127, and 127.1 follows strict statutory carryover and anti-avoidance rules. Allowable current and restored capital SR&ED expenditures added to the Subsection 37(1) pool may be deducted in the current taxation year or carried forward indefinitely to shelter future taxable income. Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs may generally be carried back 3 preceding taxation years to reduce prior Part I tax or carried forward 20 subsequent taxation years. Cash ITC refunds apply strictly to eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in the current taxation year; cash refunds cannot be claimed in respect of repayments of government assistance or contract payments, and any ITC refunded in cash is statutorily deemed to have been applied against Part I tax, reducing the ITC balance available for carryforward or carryback. Finally, where a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control, the ITA restricts both the carryforward of unused SR&ED ITCs earned before the acquisition of control and the carryback of unused SR&ED ITCs earned after the acquisition of control.
3. Qualifying Expenditures (Allowable and Qualified SR&ED Costs)
3.1 Salaries, Wages, Permissible Foreign Work, and Specified Employee Caps

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (revised January 28, 2025) and Allowable Expenditures guidance (updated October 14, 2026), allowable salaries and wages encompass the portion of employee remuneration incurred in the taxation year for SR&ED performed in Canada, provided the remuneration is paid by year-end or within 180 days after the end of the taxation year (ITA s. 78(4)). Wages unpaid after 180 days cannot be claimed in the year incurred; when subsequently paid and claimed (on Form T661 Line 310), they remain permanently excluded from the PPA salary base (ITR s. 2900(9)(b)).

Eligibility of employee activities depends on the claimant's annual overhead election. Under both the proxy and traditional methods, claimants may claim employees directly engaged in SR&ED—defined by hands-on activities rather than job titles, covering experimentation and analysis; commensurate support work in engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research; non-specialized tasks supervised by technical staff (such as operating experimental machinery or feeding raw materials); technical input in supervising SR&ED staff and administering technical contracts; technological planning and feasibility studies for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the year; and internal technical documentation. Under Subsection 2900(5) of the ITR, where "all or substantially all" (90% or more) of an employee's working time is devoted to direct SR&ED engagement, 100% of their eligible base salary enters the PPA salary base. Conversely, clerical, purchasing, or administrative staff not directly engaged in hands-on SR&ED may be claimed only as incremental overhead (Line 360) under the traditional method; under the proxy method, their wages are covered by the 55% PPA and cannot be claimed separately. For arm's-length ("other than specified") employees, cash outlays for taxable benefits, qualifying non-cash benefits (at reasonable actual cost excluding recoverable GST/HST or PST, if not expensed elsewhere), bonuses, and profit-based pay are allowable in the Section 37 pool and earn ITCs directly, but Subsection 2900(9) of the ITR excludes taxable benefits (ITA ss. 6, 7), bonuses, and profit-based remuneration from the PPA salary base for all employees.
Furthermore, a claimant may claim permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada only if all five cumulative statutory criteria are satisfied:

items: The SR&ED work is performed directly by an employee of the claimant and never by a contractor or subcontractor.
The employee was a resident of Canada at the time the wage expense was incurred.
The work was related to the business of the claimant.
The foreign work formed an integral part of, and was performed solely in support of, an SR&ED project carried out in Canada.
The salary or wages paid are not subject to an income or profits tax from another country.

body.text: Strict statutory caps govern specified employees—defined as employees who do not deal at arm's length with the claimant or who own, directly or indirectly (aggregating shares held by non-arm's-length relatives such as a spouse or sibling), 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation. Under Subsection 37(9), bonuses and remuneration based on profits for specified employees are wholly disallowed. Under Subsections 37(9.1) through 37(9.5), a specified employee's total allowable SR&ED salary is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) prorated by days employed, shared across associated corporations via Form T1174. Furthermore, when computing the 55% PPA, Subsection 2900(7) of the ITR restricts a specified employee's PPA salary base inclusion to the lesser of (a) 75% of the employee's total annual salary or wages (excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and late-paid prior-year wages) and (b) 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365), where A is the calendar-year YMPE under the Canada Pension Plan and B is days employed in the taxation year (shared as a single group ceiling across associated corporations under Subsection 2900(8), with no proration if the individual was a specified employee for only part of the year). Based on the 2026 YMPE of $74,600, 2.5 × YMPE for a full 2026 taxation year equals $186,500 (and the corresponding 2026 5 × YMPE ceiling under Subsection 37(9.1) is $373,000).
3.2 Overhead Methodologies: Traditional Method Versus 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount

Claimants must elect either the Traditional Method (ITA s. 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)) or the Proxy Method (ITA s. 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) each taxation year on Lines 160 and 162 of Form T661; the election is irrevocable once filed (ITA s. 37(10)) and defaults to the traditional method if left unselected. Under the Traditional Method, the claimant must track, allocate, and substantiate each overhead expenditure that is directly related and incremental to prosecuting SR&ED (ITR s. 2900(2)(c)) or maintaining SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment (ITR s. 2900(3))—such as incremental variable utilities, SR&ED facility/equipment repairs, clerical support wages, and current-project technological training (excluding fixed maintenance contracts, hallways, lawn care/snow removal, and recruiting or immigration fees). Provable overhead claimed under the traditional method enters both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 ITC base.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant claims zero overhead on Form T661 (deducting actual overhead as ordinary business expenses under ITA s. 9(1)) and calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible directly engaged salary base (ITR s. 2900(4)), subject to Subsection 2900(6)'s overall business-deduction cap (total business deductions less deductions under ITA sections 20, 24, 26, 30, 32, 37, 66–66.8, and 104, and less non-special-purpose building occupancy outlays). While neither the PPA nor represented overhead enters the Section 37 pool, the PPA earns full SR&ED ITCs (ITA s. 127(9))—including 100% cash refundability at 35% for CCPCs. Illustrating the 2026 break-even test from Canadian CPA practice: if a qualifying CCPC incurs $300,000 in arm's-length direct SR&ED wages, $200,000 total salary for an owner-manager spending 80% ($160,000) on SR&ED, $30,000 in materials, and $150,000 in provable incremental overhead, the Traditional Method yields $640,000 in qualified expenditures ($224,000 ITC at 35%), whereas the Proxy Method caps the owner's PPA base at $150,000 (min[$160,000; 75% × $200,000 = $150,000; $186,500]), producing a $450,000 salary base, a $247,500 PPA (55%), and $737,500 in qualified expenditures ($258,125 cash refund at 35%—or $34,125 higher than the Traditional Method, while ordinary business deductions absorb the $150,000 overhead).

body.text: 3.3 Materials Consumed or Transformed

Allowable material outlays (ITR s. 2900(2)(a); ITA s. 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V)) cover raw materials, substances, or items that compose the body of a thing at any point during the SR&ED work carried out in the taxation year, including original purchase cost plus reasonable costs required to bring the material to the location and condition needed for experimentation. Materials consumed are items destroyed, absorbed, used up, broken into small pieces, or rendered valueless by the SR&ED work, whereas materials transformed are items altered or incorporated into another material or experimental prototype while retaining some value to the claimant or another party. Crucially, materials purchased into inventory for later SR&ED work may only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed; items that do not compose the physical body of the experimental object fail the materials test and may only be considered under incremental overhead if electing the traditional method.
3.4 Arm's-Length Contracts, Non-Arm's-Length Transfers, and Third-Party Payments

External R&D outlays for work performed in Canada are divided into three distinct statutory categories (subcontractor work performed outside Canada is ineligible). First, under arm's-length contracts for SR&ED—where the payer controls the R&D, retains exclusive IP rights, typically acts as sole commercial payer, and accounts on an accrual basis—100% of the Canadian contract expenditure is deductible in the Section 37 pool, while 80% qualifies to earn SR&ED ITCs. Second, non-arm's-length SR&ED contracts are included in calculating deductible Section 37 expenditures but earn 0% ITC directly; instead, the related performer and payer may jointly file Form T1146 under Subsections 127(13)–(15) to transfer qualified expenditures incurred by the performer (provided the performer paid those outlays within 180 days after its taxation year-end and files the prescribed agreement on time). Third, third-party payments—direct funds, student/employee funding, or in-kind contributions made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, approved associations, granting councils, or eligible tax-exempt Canadian non-profit SR&ED corporations where the performer controls the basic/applied research, results are non-exclusive (with a preferential exploitation right for the claimant), and accounting follows a cash basis—are 80% eligible for SR&ED ITCs and require a separate Form T1263 for each payment.
3.5 Restored Capital Expenditures and Equipment Lease Costs (Post–December 15, 2024)

Under Bill C-15 and updated CRA policies (SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy dated June 29, 2026; SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy dated June 8, 2026; and SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy dated May 22, 2026), hardware-intensive innovators can once again claim capital and leased equipment. Expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 to acquire new or used depreciable property qualify for both the Section 37 deduction and SR&ED ITCs (on Line 390 of Form T661) if the claimant intends at acquisition that either (1) the property will be used in Canada for SR&ED during more than 90% of its operating time over its expected useful life, or (2) more than 90% of its value will be consumed in performing SR&ED in Canada. As noted in KPMG's 2026 SR&ED guidance, eligible outlays can include R&D lab and testing instruments, prototyping machinery, specialized tools and devices, experimentation infrastructure, and qualifying development software and cloud space fees. Any expenditure claimed as an SR&ED capital outlay must not be claimed on Schedule 8 (CCA). Claimants acquiring multi-use equipment below the >90% threshold should review CRA's May 22, 2026 Shared-Use-Equipment Policy alongside Class 50 / Class 53 immediate CCA expensing.

For equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, treatment depends on the overhead election. Under the Proxy Method, leased equipment (excluding general-purpose office equipment or furniture) used 90% or more of the time for SR&ED in Canada is 100% claimable as a lease cost, while equipment used primarily (more than 50% up to <90%) for SR&ED is 50% claimable. Under the Traditional Method, leased equipment used 90% or more for SR&ED is 100% claimable as a lease cost, whereas equipment used less than 90% for SR&ED is claimable only as an overhead expenditure proportional to its SR&ED usage percentage.
4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal Stacking
4.1 Post-2025 Provincial Alignment Landscape

Across Canada's 13 provinces and territories, nine provinces and Yukon provide corporate R&D tax credits that stack with federal SR&ED, whereas Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut impose no R&D-specific corporate tax credit (leaving claimants there with unreduced federal SR&ED qualified pools). According to primary Gouvernement du Québec / Revenu Québec releases and October 2026 Canadian R&D tax compliance tracking of post–Bill C-15 provincial responses, only British Columbia enacted comprehensive alignment with the federal Bill C-15 package, Québec enacted an independent commercialization overhaul, Saskatchewan enacted a targeted CCPC cap increase, and Ontario, Alberta, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon maintain independent provincial rules.

body.text: 4.2 Québec's Overhaul: The Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

Introduced in the 2025–2026 Québec Budget (tabled March 25, 2025) and effective for taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec consolidated its innovation tax system—described in legal and tax analyses as replacing eight legacy provincial measures—into the single, 100% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC). Specifically, Revenu Québec confirmed the elimination of the R&D salaries and wages credit (Form RD-1029.7-V), the university/public research centre/consortium research credit (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), the private partnership pre-competitive research credit (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), the research consortium fees and dues credit (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V, with transitional eligibility preserved for cumulative fee balances until taxation years ending no later than December 31, 2029), the technological adaptation services credit, the industrial design component of the design credits (retaining fashion design), and the income tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts. (Québec's 2025–2026 budget also modified its separate IT/AI tax rules by adding data-processing and hosting activities while removing routine maintenance or evolution, and expenses claimed under CRIC cannot be double-claimed under other Québec credits such as C3i.)

Available strictly to corporations (including corporate members of partnerships, but excluding unincorporated sole proprietorships) that carry on business and maintain an establishment in Québec, CRIC is claimed via Form RD-1029.8.CR / RD-1029.8.CR-T (while Form RD-222-V continues to track Québec R&D deductions, with consulting estimates placing Revenu Québec CRIC processing at 60–90 days). Unlike prior Québec credits that hinged on a $50 million asset threshold, CRIC rates are size-neutral across SMEs, large public corporations, and foreign subsidiaries: corporations earn 30% fully refundable on the first $1,000,000 of net qualified expenditures exceeding the annual exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations), and 20% fully refundable on all excess qualified expenditures—except that corporate partners claiming through a partnership receive only the 20% base rate without access to the 30% tier. The annual exclusion threshold equals the greater of $50,000 (prorated for short taxation years under 51 weeks) or the sum across participating employees of the Québec personal income tax basic personal amount ($18,571 in 2025 per PwC's budget summary) prorated by each employee's percentage of time devoted to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities.

Crucially, while Québec harmonizes its R&D definition with federal law and relies on the CRA to conduct the scientific review, CRIC also covers pre-commercialization activities conducted in Québec in conjunction with Québec R&D—specifically regulatory testing, technological validations, and quality-control studies for initial marketing approval/certification, plus product design (form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials). Qualified CRIC expenditures comprise 100% of eligible Québec employee wages, 50% of Québec subcontractor contracts, 50% of contracts with certified Québec universities, public research centres, or research consortia, and 100% of acquisition costs for previously unused depreciable capital property used almost exclusively in Québec R&D/pre-commercialization (excluding land, buildings, building rights, and large-investment-project tax-holiday assets), with no 55% proxy overhead uplift.
4.3 Western, Central, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes

Across the rest of Canada, October 2026 compliance tracking highlights distinct provincial rules. British Columbia expressly aligned with Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 and removed its sunset date in B.C. Budget 2026, providing a permanent 10% refundable credit to CCPCs and ECPCs up to $6,000,000 (phasing out over $15,000,000–$75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital) including restored capital expenditures, and a 10% non-refundable credit above the cap or for other corporations. Ontario retains its holdout structure: the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) applies only to CCPCs on up to $3,000,000 of Ontario current expenditures (phasing out over $500,000–$800,000 prior-year federal taxable income or $25,000,000–$50,000,000 specified capital, without confirmed capital-expenditure restoration or ECPC access), paired with the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) (3-year carryback / 20-year carryforward).

In the Prairie provinces, Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) operates independently of CCPC status, paying an 8% refundable base benefit up to the corporation's two-year rolling average Alberta R&D spend plus a 12% incremental benefit (20% combined refundable) above that historical base up to $4,000,000 annually, with updated June 30, 2026 guidance mapping lines from the revised federal Form T661. Saskatchewan doubled its CCPC refundable threshold for expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024 from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 at 10% refundable (with 10% non-refundable above $2,000,000 or for non-CCPCs including ECPCs, subject to a $1,000,000 combined annual credit cap). Manitoba provides a 15% credit covering current and eligible depreciable capital property (excluding buildings) without a $6,000,000 limit—100% refundable for contracts with qualifying Manitoba research institutes and 50% refundable / 50% non-refundable otherwise. New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland and Labrador each provide a 15% refundable R&D credit, and Yukon provides a 15% refundable credit (20% on eligible payments to Yukon University), with no confirmed comprehensive Bill C-15 alignment announced as of late October 2026.
4.4 Federal Innovation Grants and Multi-Jurisdiction Tax Credit Stacking

Direct federal and provincial R&D grants—including non-repayable contributions through the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) (renewed for clean technology in Budget 2026), the $1 billion Strategic Response Fund for large-scale R&D projects, and the $2.7 billion AI for ALL business adoption initiative announced June 4, 2026—interact with SR&ED alongside provincial R&D tax credits as government assistance under Subsections 127(18) through 127(20) of the ITA, reducing the federal qualified expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar before federal ITCs are calculated. (Whereas Bill C-15 explicitly exempted Canada Growth Fund Inc. and Canada Infrastructure Bank financing from reducing Clean Electricity ITC property costs, SR&ED continues to apply standard Section 127(18) government assistance reductions.) Notably, under ITR s. 2900(4) and (9) and ITA s. 127(9) and (18), provincial R&D tax credits reduce the overall federal qualified expenditure pool rather than reducing the employee salary base on which the 55% PPA is calculated.

To illustrate combined federal–provincial cash returns, consider a pre-revenue qualifying CCPC (below all phase-out thresholds, with no external grants) incurring $1,000,000 in 100% directly engaged Canadian R&D wages across 10 full-time arm's-length engineers in a post–March 25, 2025 taxation year and electing the 55% Proxy Method ($550,000 PPA; $1,550,000 pre-assistance federal qualified pool):

body.text: 5. Governance, Filing Compliance, Pre-Claim Approval, and Audit Procedures
5.1 Institutional Roles, Prescribed Forms, and the 18-Month Statutory Deadline

Federal tax policy design rests with the Department of Finance Canada, while operational administration, upfront technical pre-claim approvals, scientific eligibility reviews, and financial expenditure audits under the SR&ED Program Financial Claim Review Manual are conducted by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Claimants face a strict 18-month reporting deadline: businesses have 18 months after their taxation year-end to file prescribed Form T661 together with T2 Schedule 31 for corporations (or Form T2038(IND) for individuals).

To implement Bill C-15, the CRA published revised prescribed forms in May 2026, led by Form T661 (Rev. 26) issued May 15, 2026 alongside interim line instructions while Guide T4088 undergoes revision. While Part 2 project descriptions must be prepared for every claimed project, claimants may elect to submit Part 2 at filing for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, retaining remaining project narratives for CRA request. Three sets of new lines appear in Part 2 of the May 2026 Form T661: Line 207 requires the five-digit Field of Research code (RDF#####) from Statistics Canada's Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020 Version 2.0; Lines 212 and 214 record CRA pre-claim approval participation and the assigned case number; and Lines 262 and 263 require claimants claiming post–December 15, 2024 depreciable SR&ED capital property (reported on Line 390) to list up to the 10 most expensive SR&ED properties per project along with each asset's SR&ED operating-time percentage.

body.text: 5.2 Claim Preparer Disclosure and Statutory Penalty Regime

In Part 9 of Form T661, Line 935 ("Was a claim preparer engaged in any aspect of the preparation of this SR&ED claim?") and the accompanying Claim Preparer Information Table mandate granular fee transparency whenever an external advisor participates in claim preparation. Claimants must report each preparer's name, CRA Business Number, billing arrangement code, billing rate, and total fees paid or payable. Compliance is enforced through Subsections 162(5.1) and 162(5.2) of the ITA alongside updated CRA penalty policy guidelines introduced in 2025: Subsection 162(5.1) imposes a $1,000 penalty for a false statement or omission in the claim preparer information, for which the person who makes or participates in it and any claim preparer of the form are jointly and severally liable, while Subsection 162(5.2) relieves a claim preparer who exercised the degree of care, diligence and skill that a reasonably prudent person would have exercised in comparable circumstances.
5.3 Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process and AI-Driven Audit Modernization

Fulfilling Budget 2025's administrative reform mandate, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026. Through My Business Account, eligible businesses can apply before beginning R&D work or incurring costs and receive a formal upfront technical eligibility determination from the CRA within 8 weeks, supported by optional one-on-one pre-application consultations with CRA specialists (OESCPB-SVEDGPO@cra-arc.gc.ca). Furthermore, as summarized in Osler's Budget 2025 briefing, post-filing claims submitted through this elective stream that require a financial expenditure review have their processing standard cut in half from 180 days to 90 days. Concurrently, the CRA has deployed artificial intelligence risk-screening to spare low-risk claims from unnecessary audit interventions, updated The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants for pre-claim-approved files, archived legacy physician/medical professional corporation claim guidelines, and initiated consultations to streamline Form T661.
6. Scientific Eligibility Criteria, Judicial Precedents, and Compliance Protocol
6.1 Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Judicial Precedents

Every SR&ED claim rests on proving that the underlying work constitutes basic research (advancing scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view), applied research (advancing scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view), or experimental development (achieving technological advancement to create new, or incrementally improve existing, materials, products, devices, or processes), together with commensurate support work in engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research. Conversely, routine engineering and post-development commercial activities (subject to Budget 2026's proposed expansion for initial regulatory certification studies and IP protection) do not qualify.

In Canadian tax jurisprudence, courts evaluate SR&ED eligibility under the five-criteria framework established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 CTC 2520, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, and consistently applied by the Federal Court of Appeal and the Tax Court of Canada—including recent dismissals such as the 2022 Tax Court decision summarized in FitTracker, where the taxpayer's appeal failed under the Northwest Hydraulic five-criteria test. Reflecting the five Northwest Hydraulic questions, primary CRA and harmonized Québec statutory authorities confirm the core substantive elements claimants must substantiate: attempting a genuine scientific or technological advancement that cannot be resolved through routine engineering; executing rigorously organized scientific or technical work through systematic experimentation and analysis; confining claimed support tasks to commensurate statutory categories; and maintaining contemporaneous technical and financial documentation linking claimed work to allowable outlays. Where disputes arise during CRA review, claimants may utilize administrative review mechanisms (including Form RC532 where applicable), file a formal Notice of Objection within the statutory objection period, and appeal assessments to the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal (noting also appellate procedural precedent referenced in CRA roundtables such as Bozzer v. Canada (National Revenue), 2011 FCA 186).
6.2 Contemporaneous Documentation and Eight-Step Audit Readiness Protocol

items: Secure Optional Pre-Claim Approval Before Project Launch: Submit planned R&D projects through CRA My Business Account (active April 1, 2026) to obtain an 8-week upfront technical determination, qualify for 90-day expenditure reviews, and record the case number on Form T661 Lines 212 and 214.

Maintain Contemporaneous Experimental Records: Preserve real-time test logs, failed prototype analyses, engineering notebooks, and code repositories demonstrating systematic experimentation aimed at technological advancement rather than routine engineering.

Substantiate Employee SR&ED Time and Meet the 180-Day Payment Rule: Track hands-on employee engagement (documenting ≥90% ASA thresholds under ITR s. 2900(5)) separately from clerical support, and pay all accrued SR&ED wages within 180 days after year-end (ITA s. 78(4)).

Run the Annual 55% Proxy Break-Even Model: Compare provable incremental overhead (ITR s. 2900(2)(c)) against the 55% PPA (ITR s. 2900(4))—applying the 75% and 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500 for 2026) specified-employee caps—before locking in the irrevocable election on Form T661 Line 160.

Optimize the $6,000,000 Expenditure-Limit Phase-Out Election: For CCPCs with prior-year associated taxable capital above $15,000,000, test whether electing the three-year average annual gross revenue method preserves a higher share of the $6,000,000 enhanced limit, and file updated T2 Schedule 49 across associated CCPCs.

Log Operating Time for Post–December 15, 2024 Capital and Leased Assets: Document acquisition intent and machine-utilization percentages proving >90% SR&ED operating time for depreciable capital property (reported on Form T661 Lines 262, 263, and 390, and excluded from Schedule 8 CCA) and ≥90% (100% claim) or >50% (50% proxy claim) usage for leased equipment.

Track Québec CRIC and Proposed Budget 2026 Commercialization Outlays: For Québec establishments (taxation years starting after March 25, 2025), segregate pre-commercialization regulatory validation, product design, and new capital equipment on Form RD-1029.8.CR; nationwide, segregate initial regulatory certification tests and Canadian-prepared IP protection fees to capture the proposed Budget 2026 commercialization expansion.

Verify Part 9 Preparer Disclosures and File Within 18 Months: Confirm accurate claim preparer fee reporting in Part 9 of Form T661 (ITA ss. 162(5.1)–(5.2)), file non-arm's-length Form T1145 / T1146 / T1174 agreements on time, enter five-digit CRDC codes on Line 207, and transmit Form T661 and T2 Schedule 31 ahead of the 18-month statutory deadline.
